paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: God takes a promise seriously, even when we stop. The people of Jerusalem made a covenant to proclaim liberty, and then they freed their servants (Jeremiah 34:8-10). Later they took those servants right back, after making that covenant before Him in the house that bears His Name (Jeremiah 34:11, 15-16). That's not a small flip-flop. The LORD says they "profaned My name" (Jeremiah 34:16).

Now look at how the LORD answers. He reminds them of what He did first: He brought their forefathers out of Egypt, "out of the house of slavery" (Jeremiah 34:13). Freedom was never their invention to hand out and snatch back. It came from Him, so when they refused to proclaim it for their neighbors, He gave them a freedom they never asked for: "freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine!" (Jeremiah 34:17). I think that is one of the heaviest lines in the whole book.

So what do I carry out of my bakery today? I can't promise one thing in the morning and take it back by the afternoon like I'm returning a mixer with the receipt in my hand. When God shows me mercy, He wants me to pass it on to the people around me. And I keep my ovens ready, because the LORD who says what He will do, does what He says, and that is good news for everyone who walks with Him.
